newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FOCUS-Philippine Feb inflation seen at 4.94 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Philippine Feb inflation seen at 4.94 pct.

text.p: Inflation in the Philippines is expected to soften to 4.94 percent year-on-year in February from 5.0 percent in January and 11.8 percent in February last year despite an increase in oil prices, analysts said.
The forecast was the average of a Reuters poll of six financial institutions conducted at the end of the week and ahead of Wednesday's announcement of the figure.
In spite of cost-push pressures on inflation, prices have been relatively stable in February as a result of the competition spawned by a more open economy, the analysts said.

"Most manufacturers are committed to hold prices at current levels. They're more bent on raising volumes rather than prices," said Rolando Valenzuela, senior vice president of Philippine TA Securities.
"Food prices have been relatively stable. The oil price hike, which was imposed in the first week of February, was minimal," added Lito Dalit, an economist at Asian Bank.

Although the country's three oil refiners raised prices of premium gasoline when the industry was freed from government control on February 8, overall prices remained steady because the oil firms lowered prices of bunker oil, analysts said.
Petron Corp, which is 40 percent-owned by the government, acted as the market leader by setting the trend in pricing with the onset of full deregulation.
That limited any increase in oil prices, analysts said. Petron has the biggest share of the domestic market at 41.7 percent.

Cecilia Tanchoco, an economist at the Bank of the Philippine Islands, said oil prices are even forecast to soften further due to the seasonal drop in demand with the end of the winter season in the northern hemisphere.
"Inflation is going to be muted in the next three months," agreed Valenzuela of Philippine TA Securities.
Apart from an anticipated lowering of oil prices, the Central Bank has been able to contain the growth of money supply, leading to lower inflationary expectations, he said.

The Central Bank has said that M3, the broadest measure of liquidity, grew by 19.8 percent in 1996 versus the maximum 25.8 percent growth allowed under a programme agreed with the International Monetary Fund.
Moreover, an expected government budget surplus this year of 13 billion pesos, up from 6.26 billion pesos last year, should keep interest rates and prices low, economists said.
The peso had likewise remained stable even with the complete elimination of foreign exchange cover for oil imports with the onset of deregulation, analysts said.
"There was not much pressure to depreciate because foreign funds have been coming in," Valenzuela said.
The peso closed at 26.331 to the dollar at the end of February, compared with 26.349 in January.
Following were the estimates made by six financial
institutions (in percentage terms):
Asian Bank 4.6-4.8
Bank of the Philippine Islands 4.8-5.0
BNP PrimeEast Securities 5.0-5.3
Philippine TA Securities 4.7-5.1
SBC Warburg 5.0
Average 4.94
